abstract: A convenient, high-yielding, and scalable synthetic approach to the construction of 4'-vinylbenzocrown ethers has been developed, which employs a decarboxylation and cyclization strategy. Using this method, a wide-ranging class of vinylbenzocrown ethers can be efficiently obtained. The identity of the crown ethers was further established using single-crystal X-ray diffraction studies. Two of the vinylbenzocrown ethers crystallize with water, affording infinite supramolecular assemblies containing hydrogen-bonded water molecules.

sezioni.testo:
Improved Syntheses of 4’-Vinylbenzo-3n-Crown-n Ethers (n = 5-7)
Liulei Ma,a Jesus Daniel Loya,a Michael Findlater,b* and Kristin M. Hutchinsa*
aDepartment of Chemistry and Biochemistry, Texas Tech University, Lubbock TX 79409, USA;
bDepartment of Chemistry and Biochemistry, University of California Merced, Merced CA 95343, USA;
*Email: michaelfindlater@ucmerced.edu; kristin.hutchins@ttu.edu
ABSTRACT: A convenient, high-yielding, and scalable synthetic approach to the construction of 4’-vinylbenzocrown ethers has  been developed, which employs a decarboxylation and cyclization strategy. Using this method, a wide-ranging class of vinylbenzocrown ethers can be efficiently obtained. The identity of the crown ethers was further established using single crystal X-ray diffraction  studies. Two of the vinylbenzocrown ethers crystallize with water, affording infinite supramolecular assemblies containing hydrogenbonded water molecules.
Since their initial discovery by Pedersen,1 crown ethers and  related compounds have been widely applied in many different  areas of synthetic chemistry and materials science including  host-guest chemistry,2 molecular sensors,3 and phase-transfer  catalysts.4 Among the very large number of crown ethers that  are now known, 4'-vinylbenzocrown ethers are one class of  monomers that can be used for the preparation of functional polymers.5 Numerous synthetic methods have been reported that  provide access to this class of crown ethers. One early approach  reported by Smid and co-workers6 (Scheme 1a), involved a  three-step procedure starting from 3,4-dihydroxybenzaldehyde  and yielded the crown via cyclization, a Grignard reaction, and  dehydration in an overall yield of 20-23 %. Another approach  was disclosed by Matsuda and co-workers7 (Scheme 1b) and  employed monobenzo-15-crown-5 as starting material which  can, over four independent steps (nitration, reduction, diazotization, vinylation), afford the desired 4'-vinylbenzocrown ether  products in low overall yield (20-25 %). A third method was  subsequently described by Reinhoudt and co-workers8 (Scheme  1c) and used an intramolecular cyclization of catechol with tetraethylene glycol dimesylate to construct the crown ether ring.  Crown formation was followed by acetylation, reduction, and  dehydration to deliver the targeted species in poor synthetic  yield (8-38 %). All synthetic strategies, although widely applied, suffer from low overall yields, synthetically laborious  procedures, and tedious separations.
Due to our ongoing interest in the separation of metal ions,9  and our need to rapidly and reliably prepare sequestrants for  further study, we sought to develop alternative synthetic strategies to prepare 4'-vinylbenzocrown ethers. We had moderate initial success by using 3,4-dihydroxybenzaldehyde in the macrocyclization, followed by a Wittig reaction to transform the  formyl- group to a vinyl- group. However, purification of the  4'-vinylbenzo crown ethers are challenging due to the triphenylphosphine oxide formed in the reaction and distillation  to remove N,N-dimethylformamide solvent. We then formulated an alternative strategy (Scheme 1d) to introduce the vinyl  group and avoid using a Wittig olefination.
As outlined in Scheme 2, ditosyl derivatives of the oligoethylene glycols (1a, 1b, and 1c) were prepared quantitatively following the previously reported procedure of Chen and Baker.10  In a key improvement, 4-vinylbenzene-1,2-diol (2) was obtained in a convenient and high-yielding one-step protocol from  3,4-dihydroxycinnamic acid (caffeic acid) via decarboxylation,  which can be used directly in the next step after removal of triethylamine. Treatment of 1a, 1b, or 1c with 2 in the presence of  potassium carbonate, afforded the 4'-vinylbenzocrown ethers  (3a, 3b, or 3c, respectively) in excellent isolated yields and on  the gram scale. The identity of the newly prepared crowns was  confirmed using multinuclear (1H and 13C) NMR spectroscopy,  high-resolution mass spectrometry, and single-crystal X-ray  diffraction.
Scheme 1. Synthetic routes to 4'-vinylbenzocrown ethers
The most important structural feature of crown ethers and  the key to their widespread application is the central cavity with  which ‘guests’ can be accommodated. To probe this feature, we  grew single crystals of each 4'-vinylbenzo crown ether from
Scheme 2. Synthesis of 4'-vinylbenzocrown ethers using decarboxylation and cyclization
concentrated solutions, which proved suitable for analysis by  single crystal X-ray diffraction studies. A concentrated methanol solution of 3a was placed in a refrigerator (at ca. 4 °C) and  after seven days, crystals were isolated and subjected to X-ray  analysis. Diffraction studies revealed the molecular structure to  be the trihydrate of the desired crown, 3a·3H2O (Figure 1a).  Under slightly different conditions, room temperature storage  of a methanol solution of 3b for ~five days, afforded the trihydrate of 3b as a crystalline solid and its solid-state structure was  determined (Figure 1b). It proved possible to obtain a non-hydrated crystalline sample of 3b from a solution of 3b in a mixture of methanol and dichloromethane (1:1, v/v), which was left  in the fume hood for more than one month (Figure 1c). Compound 3c is a liquid at room temperature, and, thus far, we have  not been able to obtain suitable crystals for X-ray analysis.
The supramolecular assembly of the trihydrates, 3a·3H2O  and 3b·3H2O, are quite similar and constitute infinite one-dimensional chains of hydrogen-bonded water and 4'-vinylbenzo-
Figure 1. X-ray crystal structures showing the asymmetric unit of:  a) 3a·3H2O, b) 3b·3H2O, and c) 3b. Disorder in 3b·3H2O and 3b  are omitted for clarity. The oxygen atoms of the water molecules  are shown in blue.
crown ether molecules (Figures 2a and 2b). For 3a·3H2O, one  water molecule lies below the crown and donates two hydrogen  bonds to two oxygen atoms on opposite sides of the crown. The  second water molecule lies above the crown and is also engaged  in two hydrogen bonds. One acceptor is an oxygen that is attached to the benzene ring and the second oxygen lies across the  crown cavity. The third water molecule acts as a bridge between  the two water molecules lying above and below the crown to  create the infinite chain. The structure of 3b contains no water  or solvent, and involves infinite, offset stacks of 3b molecules  with all the cavities arranged in a channel-like manner (Figure  2c).
Figure 2. X-ray crystal structures highlighting supramolecular assembly of: a) 3a·3H2O, b) 3b·3H2O, and c) 3b. Disorder in  3b·3H2O and 3b are omitted for clarity. The oxygen atoms of the  water molecules are shown in blue.
In conclusion, 15-, 18-, and 21-membered 4'-vinylbenzo  crown ethers were synthesized using a convenient and scalable  synthetic strategy. Further implementation of these crown  ethers will play a key role in the fields of host-guest chemistry  and functional polymer synthesis.

General Methods. All reagents and solvents were purchased from commercial supplies and used without further purification. Analytical thin-layer chromatography (TLC) was  performed using commercial precoated silica gel plates containing a fluorescent indicator. Column chromatography was carried out using silica gel (40-63 µm). High-resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS) data were collected using a Thermo Exactive  MS with an Orbitrap mass analyzer in ESI mode. Single crystal  X-ray data were performed on a Rigaku XtaLAB SynergyiKappa diffractometer equipped with a PhotonJet-i X-ray  source operated at 50 W (50 kV, 1 mA) to generate Cu Kα radiation (λ = 1.54178 Å) and a HyPix-6000HE HPC (hybrid photon counting) detector. 1H and 13C NMR spectra were recorded  using 400 MHz spectrometers. Chemical shifts (δ) are reported  in ppm relative to residual CHCl3 (1H, δ 7.26), residual DMSO  (1H, δ 2.50), CDCl3 (13C, δ 77.16) or DMSO-d6 (13C, δ 39.52).  Data for 1H NMR spectra are reported as follows: chemical  shift, multiplicity (s = singlet, d = doublet, t = triplet, m = multiplet), coupling constant (J, Hz), and integration. Data for 13C  NMR spectra are reported in terms of chemical shift. All NMR  solvents were purchased from Cambridge Isotope Laboratories.  1a, 1b, and 1c were synthesized according to the reported  method.10 (Note: compounds 1a-1c are bis-electrophiles. Biselectrophiles are reactive species that can undergo intramolecular nucleophilic substitution and alkylate nucleotides in  DNA.11)
4-vinylbenzene-1,2-diol (2). The compound was synthesized according to the previous report12 with minor modifications. Caffeic acid (9.0 g, 50 mmol) was dissolved in 80 mL  N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF). Into this solution, triethylamine (20.8 mL, 150 mmol) and 60 mg BHT (inhibitor) were  added, and then the mixture was heated to 100 °C in an oil bath  and stirred for 12 h under N2. The reaction mixture was cooled  to room temperature and the triethylamine was removed by rotary evaporation. 2 in remaining DMF was used directly in the  next step without further purification.1H NMR (DMSO-d6, 400  MHz): δ 9.01(s, 1H), 8.89 (s, 1H), 6.85 (s, 1H), 6.75 – 6.64 (m,  2H), 6.53 (dd, J = 17.6, 10.9 Hz, 1H), 5.49 (d, J = 17.6 Hz, 1H),  5.00 (d, J = 10.9 Hz, 1H). 13C{1H} NMR (DMSO-d6, 101 MHz):  δ 145.59, 145.30, 136.77, 128.82, 118.06, 115.51, 112.89,  110.44.  General procedure for 4'-vinylbenzo crown ether preparation, example using 15-vinyl-2,3,5,6,8,9,11,12-octahydrobenzo[b][1,4,7,10,13]pentaoxacyclopentadecine (3a). Potassium carbonate (5.6 g, 40 mmol) and 2 (1.5 g, 11 mmol) in a  17.6 mL DMF solution were added to a stirred solution of tetraethylene glycol di(p-toluenesulfonate) (1a, 5.37 g, 10 mmol)  in 100 mL DMF. The resulting suspension was heated to 100  °C in an oil bath under N2 for 48 h. The reaction was cooled to  room temperature and DMF was removed by using a rotary  evaporator. The oily residue was then diluted with 400 mL  DCM and the residue was washed with 10% hydrochloric acid  solution, brine, and twice with distilled water. The organic layer  was dried with MgSO4, concentrated by rotary evaporation, and  purified by column chromatography (hexane: ethyl acetate:  methanol = 10:2:1, v:v:v) to afford a white solid (2.2 g, 75%).
